No, the field specific jargon is there to solve the purposes of the field. It doesn't make sense to outsiders because they're missing the context of the field's knowledge- the shared concepts, facts and procedures and how they fit together. Often the jargon is abbreviated to make routine communication more efficient, making the jargon seem even more incomprehensible.

Legalese is very structured and verbose because its purpose is to describe unambiguously exactly what should occur and in which exact situations. The ambiguity is resolved by defining every phrase and specific word usage so that meanings can't be quibbled over and situations and outcomes are clearly described. Add in a structured and numbered paragraph structure and paragraphs referencing other paragraphs ("in case C, do X with restrictions X.a and X.b. In case D, do X with restrictions X.b and X.c.") and you need to truly study the material to understand the shape of the situations it attempts to describe. It's complex because our society is complex and complex legal situations need describing.
As someone who studied college level math, I cannot disagree.

I'd like to point out that it's the same for "medical jargon" as well. A lot of those words that most people see as being huge and complicated are actually just made up of several small, descriptive parts based on Latin and Greek. (And then they get abbreviated because they're long.) Anybody can learn it if they want to, though.
